column4: The section's dictionary example is gold extracted from ore and its grain is separated from husk; this ayah explicitly heats material for adornment, then says its foam goes away while what benefits people remains, making the valued core versus waste separation concrete.

The section quotes the same wording as 100:10, “مَا فِي صُدُورِكُمْ,” and pairs it here with “لِيُمَحِّصَ مَا فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ”: the contents are tested and purified, a direct account of the inward sorting.
The section says the heart's kernel is what will be sifted from the chest; this ayah asks whether God will not bring out the grudges in hearts, naming an inward deposit made manifest.
The section's graves are opened and their contents scattered; this ayah repeats that exact grave-opening scene in “بُعْثِرَتِ الْقُبُورُ,” directly staging what had been buried coming out.
The section foregrounds the wording “ما في الصدور”; this ayah says whether people hide or disclose what is in their breasts, God knows it, grounding the image in knowledge of concealed contents.
The section describes chest contents being extracted; this ayah names the Day “تُبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ,” when hidden matters are tested, closely matching the disclosure and examination.

The section's named dictionary form حَبّة is grain and its chest is a collecting vessel; this ayah says God knows even a grain in earth's darkness and that it is in a clear record, joining hidden seed, concealment, and account.

The section's heart-kernel is a hidden grain inside; this ayah says even a mustard seed concealed in rock, heaven, or earth is brought by God, giving a precise image of the smallest hidden thing being recovered.

The section says sorting is fine-grained and cites the weight of a particle; this ayah places just scales and says even a mustard-seed weight is brought, explicitly joining tiny measure and final accounting.
The section invokes this ayah for the fineness of the sorting: even the weight of a particle of good is seen, so no small remainder escapes.
The section cites 99:7 for the smallest good deed; this adjacent ayah applies the same particle-weight to evil, completing the two-sided account and showing that the sorting does not spare the bad.
The section's lexicon calls the last line of an account the revealed remainder; this opened record omits neither small nor large and makes every deed present, a direct image of exhaustive reckoning.
After the graves are scattered in 82:4, this ayah says each soul learns what it sent ahead and left behind; that is the account disclosed after the buried contents emerge.
The section's “what is in the breasts” becomes an account; this ayah says whatever people disclose or conceal within themselves is reckoned by God, explicitly linking inward contents to judgment.
The section defines tahsīl as distinguishing what is obtained; this ayah says God will distinguish the foul from the good, naming the moral separation that the grain-and-chaff image makes visible.
The section presents extraction as separating kernel from refuse; this ayah says God separates foul from good and piles the foul together, giving the same sorting an explicit moral outcome.

The section's grain is extracted from husk; this ayah speaks of what God brings from the earth and forbids choosing its bad portion to give away, making quality-selection in produce a concrete moral boundary.

The section's dictionary entry links حبّ to grain and notes husk and fragrant seeds; this ayah names “الْحَبُّ ذُو الْعَصْفِ وَالرَّيْحَانُ,” putting grain, its husk, and fragrant growth in one agricultural scene.

The section's dictionary form حَبّة is a grain kernel; this ayah names God as “فَالِقُ الْحَبِّ وَالنَّوَىٰ,” splitting grain and date-stone, a direct physical parallel to opening a shell to reach its core.
The section contrasts inward knowledge with outward appearance; this ayah pairs what the eyes betray with what breasts hide, showing how the visible surface can differ from the concealed interior.
The section treats the chest as a vessel in which matters stay hidden; this ayah describes people folding their breasts to hide from God, then says He knows what they conceal and declare.
The section says concealed heart-contents will be brought out; this ayah has hypocrites fear a surah that will tell them what is in their hearts, a specific disclosure of inner contents.
The section cites the dictionary opposition of inward face and outward appearance; this ayah explicitly names the outward and inward forms of sin and says those who commit it will be repaid.
The section's inside/outside distinction is explicit here: hostility has appeared from mouths, while what breasts conceal is greater, so the inner contents exceed their visible trace.
The section's chest is a hidden store; this ayah contrasts speaking secretly and aloud, then says God knows what is within breasts, directly connecting concealment with divine knowledge.

The section identifies خبير as knowledge of an affair's inward parts; following 67:13's hidden breasts, this ayah asks whether the Creator knows and calls Him “الْخَبِيرُ,” making that inward knowledge explicit.
The section's sorting uncovers what was in the chest; this ayah says people will be presented on that day with no hidden thing among them, a direct boundary of complete exposure.
The section stages hidden contents being brought out; this ayah describes people standing exposed so nothing about them is hidden from God, carrying the same disclosure into the Day of account.
The section describes an account's contents being brought to light; this ayah says each person's record will be brought out on the Resurrection Day, open before them.
After the personal record is produced in 17:13, this ayah commands, “اقْرَأْ كِتَابَكَ,” and says the person is enough as their own reckoner, completing the accounting scene.
The section's final account lays open what was hidden; this ayah says the written sheets are unfolded, giving the record itself an image of disclosure.
After the records are unfolded in 81:10, this ayah says each soul knows what it brought, stating the result of the disclosure in the person's own account.
The section pictures a final account being collected and exposed; this ayah places the record at judgment and says the dispute is settled justly, staging the reckoning.
After the book is placed in 39:69, this ayah says each soul is paid in full for what it did and God knows what they do, completing the account and the knowledge behind it.
The section's account brings inner and outer deeds to judgment; this ayah says every community is called to its book on the day of judgment, a concrete record-based reckoning.

After communities are called to their books in 45:28, this ayah says the record speaks truth about them and that their deeds were being written down, specifying how the account preserves what was done.
The section describes a final tally of what remains from deeds; this ayah says a person will be told what they sent ahead and left behind, an explicit accounting of the inwardly accumulated record.
The section says what is inside is ultimately brought out; this ayah says a person is a witness against themself, so inner truth remains visible even if excuses are offered.
Following the self-witness in 75:14, this ayah says excuses do not conceal the truth, a direct limit on hiding what the account has exposed.
The section links the grave to what stays buried until the appointed opening; this ayah says the earth casts out its burdens, directly staging concealed contents emerging from the ground.
The section's grave image is a covered state that later opens; this ayah says the earth will report its news, making the ground itself disclose what it has held.
The section says what is in graves is brought out; this ayah states that God raises those in the graves, a direct formulation of the same resurrection scene.
The section pairs graves with the chest's hidden contents; this ayah says God knows what the earth diminishes from the dead and has a preserving record, joining burial with preserved accounting.
The section's graves open at resurrection; this ayah says the earth splits open over the dead as they hurry out, directly staging emergence from burial.
The section's opening of graves is matched by this ayah's people hastening from the tombs toward their Lord after the trumpet.
The section stages those in graves being brought out; this ayah says people will emerge quickly from the graves, an explicit parallel scene.
The section's graves are opened; this ayah depicts people coming out of the graves like scattered locusts, a direct image of the resurrection's dispersal.

The section treats the chest as a container whose contents are extracted; this ayah says the earth throws out what is within it and empties itself, a close nonhuman parallel to disclosure from a container.

The section contrasts hidden inward condition with visible appearance; after 47:29's grudges brought out, this ayah says the Prophet could recognize people by their marks and speech, showing outward signs disclose an interior state.
The section's 3:154 uses the purification verb “لِيُمَحِّصَ” for hearts; this earlier Uhud passage says God purifies the believers, using the same verb for the larger testing process.
The section makes what is hidden in the chest the object of final knowledge; this ayah contrasts public speech with what people conceal and says God knows both.

The section says chests contain matters that will be exposed; this ayah says God knows what people hide and disclose and is “عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ,” directly naming knowledge of their inner contents.
The section contrasts a hidden inward face with outward appearance; this ayah says the Lord knows what breasts conceal and what people disclose.
This repeated formulation says the Lord knows what breasts conceal and what is declared, directly matching the section's inward/outward distinction in another occurrence.
The section joins knowledge of the chest with the return and account; this ayah says people return to God, are told what they did, and that He knows what is in breasts.

The section's last word is خبير, one who knows an affair's inward reality; this ayah asks each soul to inspect what it sent ahead for tomorrow and says God is “خَبِيرٌ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ,” joining forethought, deed, and knowledge.

The section's dictionary form حَبّة is grain as the kernel of the heart; this ayah makes one grain grow seven ears, each with a hundred grains, turning that kernel into a concrete image of multiplied provision.
The section's dictionary image separates grain from husk; this ayah depicts rain-grown vegetation becoming dry chaff scattered by wind, supplying the discarded plant matter in that image.

After 18:45's chaff is scattered, this ayah contrasts worldly wealth and children with “الْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ,” the lasting remainder, making the section's lexical sense of what remains explicit.
After the earth reports its news in 99:4, this ayah says its Lord has inspired it to do so; it supplies the cause of that disclosure in the passage about earth's hidden contents.
After the dead come from the tombs in 36:51, this ayah has them ask who raised them from their resting place, completing the grave-opening scene with recognition of resurrection.
The section's grave image is a body hidden in earth and later brought out; this ayah says humanity is returned to earth and then brought out from it again.
This ayah gives the burial side of the section's buried-then-raised sequence: God causes a person to die and be buried, the concealed state that 100:9 reverses.

Continuing the passage about inner grudges in 47:29, this ayah says people will be tested until those who strive and endure are known and their reports tested, linking trial with what becomes known about them.
After 3:154 describes the Uhud trial of what is in believers' chests, this ayah names those who turned away and says it was because of what they had earned, connecting hidden state to enacted deeds.
The section describes an inner core being sifted and purified; this ayah says success belongs to the one who purifies the soul, a specific moral counterpart to extraction.
The section's buried inner contents are brought out for judgment; this next ayah says the soul is lost when it is “دَسَّاهَا,” buried or obscured, the contrary outcome to purification in 91:9.
The section's khabīr is knowledge of inward affairs; this ayah pairs the return to God and report of deeds with “عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ,” joining hidden states to the final account.

The section defines خبير as knowing an affair's inner reality rather than its appearance; this ayah says honor rests on taqwa rather than tribe and ends with “عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌ,” placing God's measure beyond visible lineage.
The section stages resurrection followed by disclosure of deeds; this ayah says death will meet those who flee it, then they return to the Knower of unseen and seen and are told what they did.
The section's final image is the Lord's khabīr knowledge at the day of reckoning; this ayah names the trumpet's blowing and calls God “الْحَكِيمُ الْخَبِيرُ,” tying that knowledge to resurrection.
The section asks what is in the chest to be brought out; this Uhud ayah contrasts what people say with what is not in their hearts and what they conceal, a specific outer/inner mismatch.
The section's chest image concerns concealed inward matter; this ayah asks whether hypocrites know God knows their secret and private talk, identifying what they try to keep hidden.
The section names حبّ as grain and the separation of grain from straw; this ayah names “حَبَّ الْحَصِيدِ,” harvested grain, in a scene of rain and crops.
The section's grain is what is recovered from plant matter; this ayah describes grain coming out of green growth as “حَبًّا مُتَرَاكِبًا,” a concrete crop image.
The section describes grain separated from its husk; this ayah tells the people to leave what they reap in its ears, a specific case where grain is deliberately kept within its husk for storage.
The section's kernel-and-chaff image depends on cultivated grain; this ayah asks what people sow, establishing the seed whose growth and fate are considered in its neighboring verses.
After the sowing question in 56:63, this ayah asks whether people make the crop grow or God, connecting grain's yield to provision beyond human control.
Following the crop-growth question, this ayah says God could make the crop dry debris; it gives the discarded, vanishing plant side of the section's grain-versus-chaff separation.
The section identifies the dictionary form حَبّ as grain; this ayah names grain among the produce brought out of the earth, placing the word in a concrete provision scene.
The section's dictionary form حَبّ is grain; this ayah says rain brings forth grain and vegetation, another direct crop scene for the word's seed sense.

The section distinguishes what is fit to remain from husk; this ayah contrasts good land, whose growth comes forth, with bad land yielding only scant growth, a concrete boundary of good and poor produce.
The section's threshing image removes the husk to keep the grain; this ayah shows growth turning yellow and then to debris, the contrary case where the plant's remainder is worthless chaff.
The section's grain image begins in cultivated growth; this ayah says God brings forth pasture, the living growth that the next ayah shows becoming chaff.
After pasture is brought forth in 87:4, this ayah says it becomes dark chaff, a specific image of the plant residue that contrasts with the kernel retained in the section.

The section distinguishes the lasting kernel from what is discarded; this ayah follows vegetation from growth to yellowing and chaff, then calls worldly life deceptive provision, a specific reversal in which the whole crop passes away.
The section's dictionary gloss says the remainder stays firm after the rest goes; this ayah says everyone on earth passes away, establishing what does not last.
Following 55:26's passing away, this ayah says the face of the Lord remains, a direct formulation of what stays after everything else goes.
The section's account asks what remains once other things pass; this ayah contrasts worldly provision and adornment with what is with God as better and more lasting.
The section's dictionary sense of what remains is stated here as the Hereafter being “خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ,” the lasting counterpart to what is loved and gathered in worldly life.

The section juxtaposes the root ح ب ب in love with its dictionary form حَبّة for grain; this ayah intensifies the love of wealth with “حُبًّا جَمًّا,” reinforcing the passion half of the kernel-in-the-heart image.

The section links love of wealth with the grain/kernel sense of ح ب ب and separately uses gold from ore as its extraction image; this ayah places “حُبُّ الشَّهَوَاتِ” beside accumulated gold and silver, concretely joining intense attachment and valued metal.
The section says a bird's crop is a collecting pouch because it gathers food; this ayah describes a person who gathered and hoarded, a concrete human counterpart to the chest as a store.
The section's bird-crop dictionary image gathers what is taken in; this ayah says a person amasses wealth and counts it, connecting accumulation in the chest with the intense love of wealth in 100:8.

The section turns the root ح ب ب from love of wealth toward the heart's inner attachment; this ayah contrasts people who love their rivals with believers whose love for God is stronger, showing a contrary object for the heart's love.
The section depicts strong love of wealth as a kernel in the chest; this ayah says righteousness is not reached until one spends what one loves, turning that attachment toward relinquishment.

The section contrasts the inner reality with outward appearance; this ayah says sacrificial flesh and blood do not reach God but taqwa does, a precise reversal in which inward quality matters beyond the visible offering.

The section describes the final account as what remains from calculation; this ayah says the weighing on that day is true and distinguishes those whose scales are heavy, making the account's measure explicit.
After the true weighing in 7:8, this ayah names the light scales and their loss, the contrary result of the final sorting.
The section's image makes the final account a careful sorting; this ayah says those whose scales are heavy will succeed, explicitly weighing what each person brought.
After the heavy scales in 23:102, this ayah gives the opposite result for those whose scales are light, completing the separation of outcomes.
The section describes the account as a final collected remainder; this ayah weighs deeds and names the one whose scales are heavy, directly staging that measure.
After the heavy scales in 101:6, this ayah gives the successful person's outcome, completing the favorable side of the measured account.
The section's extraction separates what remains good from refuse; this ayah gives the opposite case of light scales.
After the light scales in 101:8, this ayah names the person's destination, completing the contrary outcome of the account.
The section's final disclosure exposes what has been gathered within; this ayah gives the one who receives the record in the right hand a concrete form of the revealed account.
After receiving the record in 84:7, this ayah says the person will have an easy reckoning, directly joining the record to the account.
The section says no inward remainder escapes the final account; this ayah gives the contrary case of the person who receives the record behind the back.

The section links the root ح ب ب in love with the kernel stored in the heart; this ayah has the righteous give food “عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ.” That phrase can mean despite loving it or for love of God, so either reading turns a valued thing toward giving rather than hoarding.
